To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the teacher/student discourse binary is a powerful and pervasive discourse that is embedded in and shapes classroom interactions, and it is not the sole responsibility of the teacher to disrupt this binary.
teachers’ classroom discourse is shaped by their own beliefs about teaching and learning and by the ways in which they view the teacher and student roles.
teachers’ classroom discourse is shaped by the binary of teacher/student.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the ways in which teachers and students are discursively constructed as separate, oppositional, and unequal.
the discursive construction of the classroom teacher as a person who is always in the know, always in control, and always the expert.
the ways in which the discursive binary teacher/student is constructed, maintained and deconstructed in classroom discourse.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the teacher is not a teacher and the student is not a student.
teachers’ classroom discourse is not only an indicator of their pedagogical practice but also a means of constructing the teacher/student binary.
the teacher/student binary is not a fixed, natural or necessary relationship.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we are trying to help students understand that the way they think about mathematics and the ways that they are taught are not natural, but socially constructed.
the research is about how to make sense of the discursive practices of mathematics classrooms, and how those discursive practices are connected to the social practices of mathematics classrooms.
we are interested in how teachers and students talk about mathematics and what they talk about.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the teacher/student binary can be a barrier to student learning, and that it is important for teachers to reflect on their use of the binary and how they can deconstruct it.
teachers’ classroom discourse can be improved when teachers reflect on their own practice.
teachers can be reflective and critical about their own teaching, but that this is a process that requires support.
